name: Printing Sequence of Numbers with a Gap Between Adjacent Values (Case 2)
description: Construct a program that prints a sequence of numbers from 7 (inclusive) to 35 (inclusive) in increments of 7.
code:
#Step 1: Iterate through the numbers in the sequence
for num in range(7, 36, 7): 
    #Step 1.1: Print each number in the sequence
    print(num)

commentList: You use this for-loop to run the same indented block once for each number in the sequence; on each iteration the current value is stored in the variable num.
range(7, 36, 7) creates the sequence starting at 7, increasing by 7 each time, and stopping before 36 — so the values you get are 7, 14, 21, 28, 35.
Because the range stop is exclusive, you must use 36 (not 35) to include 35; if you used range(7, 35, 7) you would miss the final 35.
Watch the syntax: the line must end with a colon and the following print line must be indented. Forgetting the colon or wrong indentation causes a SyntaxError or IndentationError.
Be careful with the step value: step cannot be 0 (that raises ValueError), and passing non-integers to range will raise a TypeError.
For clarity and good style, pick a descriptive loop variable name (num is fine here), avoid modifying num inside the loop, and add a short comment if the sequence logic might be unclear to readers.

commentList: You use print(num) to display the current value of num so the program outputs 7, 14, 21, 28, 35 — one value per loop iteration.
You are calling the print function with num as its argument; in Python 3 the parentheses are required and print writes the value to the screen followed by a newline by default.
Because this line is indented inside the for loop, you will print a value on every iteration; if you un-indent it, you'll only print once after the loop finishes.

Common mistakes: writing print num (Python 2 style) will cause a SyntaxError in Python 3, forgetting to define num will cause a NameError, and thinking print modifies num is wrong — it only outputs the value.

Best practice: for simple output print(num) is fine; if you want different formatting use print(num, end=' ') for same-line output or build a string (e.g., ' '.join(map(str, ...))) when you need controlled formatting or fewer print calls.

distractors.description: Step-by-step why you might pick this: you correctly recognize the start (7) and the step (7), and you assume the listed end (35) should be used directly as the last value. The common mistaken belief is that the stop argument in the range is included. What actually happens if you use this line: the loop will generate 7, 14, 21, and 28, but it will stop before reaching the provided stop boundary, so 35 is not produced. There's no runtime error — the program simply omits the final expected number. You might choose this because it feels natural to put the last number you want as the stop value. The key problem is that the stop parameter is treated as a boundary that the sequence does not reach, so this line fails to include the intended final value.

Step-by-step why you might pick this: you remember the start and the end values but forget the step, or you think Python will automatically pick the step needed to get the desired multiples. If you run this line, the loop will produce every integer from 7 up to 35 (7, 8, 9, ..., 35). The program will run without errors, but the output will include a lot of extra numbers instead of just the multiples of 7. You might choose this because it's shorter and you assume the interpreter will do the rest, but the missing step means you get step=1 behavior, which is not what the task asks for.

Step-by-step why you might pick this: you realize you need a third argument for stepping, but you accidentally type 6 because you miscounted or confused the interval. With this line, the loop produces 7, 13, 19, 25, 31 and then stops before reaching 36, so 35 is never printed and most values are not multiples of 7. The code runs normally, but the output is wrong because the step you chose doesn't match the required spacing between elements. You might be tempted to use 6 if you incorrectly calculate differences, but that leads to the wrong sequence and misses the expected numbers.
